title: Physics
summary: SI units and instruments, laws of motion, gravitation, fluids, heat, sound, light, electricity, EM waves, nuclear physics and famous inventions. CGL asks 1-2 questions — mostly units, instruments and 'which principle explains this everyday effect'.

subtopics.title: SI units, conversions and measuring instruments
subtopics.concept: Every measurement has a number and a unit. The world uses one agreed system, the **SI system**, which has seven base units. All other units are built from these seven. Exams ask many recall questions here: named units, practical units and instruments.

tricks.title: Base units in one line
tricks.body: Say it as **M**etre, **K**ilogram, **S**econd, **A**mpere, **K**elvin, **M**ole, **C**andela. Anything not on this list is derived.

example.q: Which of these is NOT an SI base unit: kelvin, candela, newton, mole?
steps: List the seven base units: m, kg, s, A, K, mol, cd.
Kelvin, candela and mole are on the list.
Newton is not on the list.

tricks.title: Read the root of the instrument name
tricks.body: **Hygro** is humidity. **Hydro** is liquid density. **Lacto** is milk. **Anemo** is wind. **Sphygmo** is pulse and blood pressure. **Pyro** is fire, so high temperature. **Seismo** is earthquake.

mistakes.wrong: Treating the light year as a unit of time.
mistakes.right: A light year is a distance: about 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m.

mistakes.wrong: Calling kWh a unit of power.
mistakes.right: kWh is energy. Power is measured in watt.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing up the hygrometer and the hydrometer.
mistakes.right: Hygro means humidity. Hydro means liquid density.

mistakes.wrong: Writing the unit of temperature as "degree kelvin".
mistakes.right: Say kelvin, symbol K.

mistakes.wrong: Calling momentum, velocity or density base quantities.
mistakes.right: Only seven are base. These are derived from them.

subtopics.notes:
### The seven base units
A measurement needs a number and a unit. "The rod is 5" means nothing. "The rod is 5 metres" does.

The **SI system** (Système International, adopted in 1960) has exactly seven base quantities. They do not depend on any other quantity.

| Quantity | SI unit | Symbol |
|---|---|---|
| Length | metre | m |
| Mass | kilogram | kg |
| Time | second | s |
| Electric current | ampere | A |
| Temperature | kelvin | K |
| Amount of substance | mole | mol |
| Luminous intensity | candela | cd |

> **Watch:** The unit of temperature is the kelvin, not "degree kelvin". Newton, joule and volt are not base units.

### Derived units with names
Every other quantity is built from the seven base ones. Many derived units carry a scientist's name.

| Quantity | Unit | Quantity | Unit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Force | newton (N) | Electric charge | coulomb (C) |
| Work, energy, heat | joule (J) | Potential difference | volt (V) |
| Power | watt (W) | Resistance | ohm (Ω) |
| Pressure | pascal (Pa) | Capacitance | farad (F) |
| Frequency | hertz (Hz) | Inductance | henry (H) |
| Magnetic field | tesla (T) | Magnetic flux | weber (Wb) |
| Power of a lens | dioptre (D) | Radioactivity | becquerel (Bq) |
| Luminous flux | lumen | Illuminance | lux |
| Sound level | decibel (dB) | Speed of ships | knot |

Some units are built from base units. Force is kg·m/s², power is J/s, pressure is N/m², and frequency is 1/s. The dioptre is 1/metre. Momentum is kg·m/s, velocity is m/s, acceleration is m/s² and density is kg/m³.

### Practical units and their values
Some units are not SI, but exams love them. Learn what each one measures.

| Unit | Measures | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Light year | Distance, not time | about 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m |
| Parsec | Distance | about 3.26 light years |
| Astronomical unit (AU) | Distance | mean Earth–Sun distance, about 1.5 × 10¹¹ m |
| Ångström | Wavelength | 10⁻¹⁰ m |
| Fermi | Nuclear size | 10⁻¹⁵ m |
| Nautical mile | Distance at sea | 1852 m |
| Knot | Speed of ships and aircraft | one nautical mile per hour |
| Fathom | Depth of water | 6 feet |
| Carat | Weight of gems | 200 mg |
| Horsepower | Power | about 746 W |
| Calorie | Heat | about 4.186 J |
| Electron volt | Energy | about 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J |
| Kilowatt-hour | Energy | 3.6 × 10⁶ J |
| Bar | Pressure | 10⁵ Pa |
| Atmosphere | Pressure | about 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa |

For gold, "carat" means purity. 24 carat gold is pure.

> **Watch:** Words like "year" and "hour" inside a unit name do not make it a unit of time. A light year is distance. A kilowatt-hour is energy.

### Scalars and vectors
A **scalar** has only size. Examples: mass, speed, distance, time, work, energy, power and temperature.

A **vector** has size and direction. Examples: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum and weight.

> **Tip:** Ask if "towards the north" makes sense with the quantity. If it does, the quantity is a vector.

### Quick conversions
1. **km/h to m/s:** multiply by $\dfrac{5}{18}$. So 36 km/h is 10 m/s. Reverse it (m/s to km/h) by multiplying by $\dfrac{18}{5}$.
2. **Electricity units:** units (kWh) = watts × hours ÷ 1000. A 100 W bulb used for 10 hours uses 1 unit.

The reason is simple. 1 km is 1000 m and 1 hour is 3600 s. So 1 km/h is $\dfrac{1000}{3600} = \dfrac{5}{18}$ m/s.

> **Rule:** One "unit" on your electricity bill is 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. It is energy, not power.

### Instruments and what they measure
Most names carry a Greek root that gives the job away.

| Instrument | Measures |
|---|---|
| Barometer | Atmospheric pressure |
| Manometer | Pressure of gases |
| Hygrometer | Relative humidity |
| Hydrometer | Relative density of liquids |
| Lactometer | Purity (density) of milk |
| Anemometer | Wind speed |
| Altimeter | Altitude (aircraft) |
| Ammeter | Current (connect in series) |
| Voltmeter | Potential difference (connect in parallel) |
| Galvanometer | Detects small currents |
| Seismograph | Earthquake waves |
| Sphygmomanometer | Blood pressure |
| Pyrometer | Very high temperature (furnaces) |
| Fathometer or SONAR | Depth of the sea (echo sounding) |
| Odometer / Speedometer | Distance run / speed of a vehicle |
| Tachometer | Rotation speed (rpm) |
| Audiometer | Hearing |
| Crescograph | Growth of plants |

patterns.name: SI unit of a physical quantity
patterns.howToSpot: The question says 'The SI unit of pressure / charge / magnetic flux / power is ...' or 'which pair is wrongly matched'.
steps: Decide if the quantity is one of the 7 base quantities.
If it is derived, recall its named unit: N, J, W, Pa, Hz, C, V, Ω, F, Wb, T, H.
If it has no named unit, build it from base units (momentum is kg·m/s).
patterns.why: Every unit is fixed by international agreement, so recall plus elimination is the method.

example.q: The SI unit of magnetic field (magnetic flux density) is:
steps: Weber is the unit of magnetic flux.
Magnetic field is flux per square metre.
That unit is the tesla.

patterns.name: Instrument and what it measures
patterns.howToSpot: An instrument name ending in '-meter' or '-graph' is given and its use is asked, or the reverse.
steps: Break the name into its root: hygro, hydro, anemo, baro, seismo, sphygmo.
Pick the option that fits the root.
Watch the pairs: hygrometer and hydrometer, manometer and sphygmomanometer.
patterns.why: Most names are Greek roots that describe the job.

example.q: An altimeter is used to measure:
steps: Alti means height.
It works like a barometer.
Pressure falls as height rises.

patterns.name: Practical and astronomical units
patterns.howToSpot: Units like light year, parsec, AU, knot, nautical mile, fathom, horsepower, carat or kWh appear in 'is a unit of ...' or 'equals ...'.
steps: Sort the unit by quantity: light year, parsec, AU, fathom and nautical mile are distance.
Knot is speed. kWh, calorie and eV are energy. Horsepower is power.
Recall the value: 1852 m, 746 W, 3.6 × 10⁶ J.
patterns.why: The words 'year' and 'hour' in a unit name mislead students. The quantity decides.

example.q: A parsec is a unit of:
steps: It is used for star distances.
1 parsec is about 3.26 light years.
So it measures distance.

patterns.name: Base or derived unit; scalar or vector
patterns.howToSpot: The question says 'Which is NOT a fundamental unit', 'which is a vector' or 'which pair are both scalars'.
steps: Base units: metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole, candela. All else is derived.
Vector test: does direction change the meaning?
Speed, distance, mass, work, energy, power and time are scalars.
patterns.why: A scalar has only size. A vector needs a direction too.

example.q: Which of the following is a scalar quantity? (a) Force (b) Momentum (c) Work (d) Displacement
steps: Force needs a direction.
Momentum and displacement need a direction.
Work has only size.

patterns.name: Unit conversion and energy-bill numericals
patterns.howToSpot: A speed in km/h must be converted, or appliance watts and hours must become kWh.
steps: For speed, multiply km/h by 5/18 to get m/s.
For bills, use watts × hours ÷ 1000 to get units.
Multiply units by the rate to get rupees.
Check the size: a 1 kW appliance for 1 hour is exactly 1 unit.

example.q: Convert 54 km/h to m/s.
steps: Multiply by $\dfrac{5}{18}$.

revision: The 7 base units are m, kg, s, A, K, mol and cd.
Light year, parsec and AU are distances. Nautical mile is 1852 m. A knot is one nautical mile per hour.
1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J and it is energy. 1 horsepower is about 746 W.
Scalars: speed, work, energy, power. Vectors: velocity, force, momentum, displacement.
Hygro is humidity, hydro is liquid density, lacto is milk, anemo is wind, sphygmo is blood pressure.

subtopics.title: Motion, gravitation, work-energy, fluids and levers
subtopics.concept: Motion, force, gravity, energy, fluids and levers make up this subtopic. Exams ask which law or principle explains an everyday event. Learn each law with one example, plus the key numbers for gravity and energy.

formulas.name: First equation of motion
formulas.note: v is final speed, u is initial speed, a is acceleration, t is time

formulas.name: Kinetic and potential energy
formulas.note: m is mass, v is speed, h is height

tricks.title: Lever class from the middle item
tricks.body: Whatever sits in the middle decides the class. **F** is 1, **L** is 2, **E** is 3.

example.q: A wheelbarrow is which class of lever?
steps: The wheel is the fulcrum, at one end.
The handles are the effort, at the other end.
The load sits in the middle.

tricks.title: Squares in energy
tricks.body: KE depends on $v^2$. Double the speed and KE is 4 times. Triple it and KE is 9 times. Momentum only doubles when speed doubles.

mistakes.wrong: Saying mass changes on the Moon.
mistakes.right: Mass stays the same. Only weight becomes about one-sixth.

mistakes.wrong: Thinking g is greatest at the equator.
mistakes.right: g is greatest at the poles and least at the equator.

mistakes.wrong: Explaining rocket motion with the first law.
mistakes.right: It is the third law (action and reaction).

mistakes.wrong: Saying work is done by holding a heavy box still.
mistakes.right: There is no displacement, so the work is zero.

mistakes.wrong: Placing tongs in class 2 because they hold a load.
mistakes.right: The effort is in the middle, so they are class 3.

subtopics.notes:
### Motion in simple words
A body is in motion when its position changes with time.

- **Distance** is the total path covered. It is a scalar.
- **Displacement** is the straight-line gap from start to end, with direction. It is a vector.
- **Speed** is distance ÷ time. **Velocity** is displacement ÷ time.
- **Acceleration** is the rate of change of velocity. Its unit is m/s².

Walk once round a circular park. The distance is large but the displacement is zero.

### Newton's three laws
| Law | Statement | Everyday example |
|---|---|---|
| First (inertia) | A body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless an outside force acts. | Passengers jerk forward when a bus brakes. Dust leaves a beaten carpet. |
| Second | Force = mass × acceleration, $F = ma$. It is also the rate of change of momentum. | A cricketer pulls his hands back while catching. |
| Third | Every action has an equal and opposite reaction. | Rocket, gun recoil, swimming, walking. |

**Momentum** is $p = mv$. It stays constant when no outside force acts. That is why a gun recoils when it fires.

More on the first law: mass measures inertia. Passengers fall forward when a moving bus brakes (inertia of motion). They fall backward when a stopped bus starts suddenly (inertia of rest).

> **Tip:** Pulling the hands back while catching a ball increases the time of impact. So the force on the hands is smaller. Cars use air bags and crumple zones for the same reason.

### Gravitation
Every two masses attract each other. Newton's law is $F = \dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$, with $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$ N m² kg⁻². Near the Earth this pull gives $g = 9.8$ m/s².

- g is greatest at the poles and least at the equator.
- g falls with height and with depth. It is zero at the Earth's centre.
- **Mass** never changes. **Weight** is $mg$ and changes with place.
- On the Moon, weight is about $\dfrac{1}{6}$ of the Earth value. A 60 kg person still has a mass of 60 kg.
- Escape velocity from Earth is about 11.2 km/s. Orbital velocity near the surface is about 7.9 km/s.
- A geostationary satellite orbits about 36,000 km above the equator with a period of 24 hours.
- Astronauts in orbit feel weightless because they are in free fall with the spacecraft.

> **Watch:** Mass is in kilogram and stays fixed. Weight is in newton and changes.

### Work, energy and power
**Work** is $W = Fs\cos\theta$. It is zero if there is no displacement or if the force is at right angles to the motion. A satellite in circular orbit is an example of zero work.

- **Kinetic energy** is $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$. Double the speed and KE becomes 4 times.
- **Potential energy** is $mgh$.
- **Power** is work ÷ time. Its unit is the watt.

Energy only changes form. A falling stone turns PE into KE.

| Device | Energy change |
|---|---|
| Electric motor | Electrical to mechanical |
| Dynamo or generator | Mechanical to electrical |
| Battery | Chemical to electrical |
| Solar cell | Light to electrical |
| Microphone | Sound to electrical |
| Loudspeaker | Electrical to sound |

### Fluids
Pressure is force ÷ area. A knife is sharp because a small area gives high pressure.

| Principle | Idea | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Pascal's law | Pressure on an enclosed liquid spreads equally | Hydraulic lift, brakes, press |
| Archimedes' principle | Upthrust = weight of liquid displaced | Ships, hydrometer, lactometer, submarines |
| Bernoulli's principle | Faster flow means lower pressure | Aeroplane lift, roofs blown off, atomiser |
| Surface tension | The surface acts like a stretched skin | Round drops, insects on water |
| Capillarity | Liquid rises in thin tubes | Lamp wick, blotting paper, plant xylem |
| Viscosity | Internal friction of a fluid | Honey flows slowly |

Ice floats because its density (about 0.92 g/cm³) is less than water's. A body floats if its density is less than the liquid's. A ship floats because its shape displaces a lot of water. Soap and kerosene lower surface tension. Kerosene on ponds kills mosquito larvae. Liquid viscosity falls when heated.

### Levers
A lever has a **fulcrum**, a **load** and an **effort**. The class depends on which one sits in the middle.

| Class | In the middle | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Class 1 | Fulcrum | Seesaw, scissors, pliers, crowbar, beam balance |
| Class 2 | Load | Nutcracker, wheelbarrow, bottle opener, lemon squeezer |
| Class 3 | Effort | Tongs, forceps, tweezers, fishing rod, human forearm, broom |

> **Rule:** Fulcrum, Load, Effort in the middle gives class 1, 2, 3. Class 2 always gives mechanical advantage. Class 3 gives speed and control.

patterns.name: Everyday event and Newton's law
patterns.howToSpot: A daily-life story (bus braking, rocket, gun recoil, cricketer catching, carpet beating) with the laws as options.
steps: If a body resists a change in rest or motion, choose the first law.
If force is reduced by taking more time, or the question uses F = ma, choose the second law.
If you push one way and move the other way (rocket, recoil, swimming), choose the third law.
patterns.why: Each law explains one kind of effect, and the story tells you which.

example.q: When a carpet is beaten with a stick, the dust comes out. This is due to:
steps: The carpet moves suddenly.
The dust tends to stay at rest.
That is inertia of rest.

patterns.name: Gravitation, weight and satellites
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks about g at poles, equator or centre, weight on the Moon, escape velocity, geostationary orbit or weightlessness.
steps: Mass is fixed. Weight changes with g.
g is larger at the poles than at the equator. It falls up and down, and is zero at the centre.
Recall the numbers: g 9.8 m/s², escape velocity 11.2 km/s, geostationary period 24 h at about 36,000 km.
patterns.why: Weight is mass times g, so only g changes from place to place.

example.q: A body has a mass of 30 kg on Earth. What is its mass on the Moon?
steps: Mass does not depend on place.
Only the weight falls to about one-sixth.

patterns.name: Fluid principle and its use
patterns.howToSpot: A device or effect (hydraulic brake, floating ship, aeroplane lift, lamp wick, round raindrop) with principles as options.
steps: Enclosed liquid and multiplied force point to Pascal.
Floating, sinking or upthrust points to Archimedes.
Fast air and low pressure point to Bernoulli.
A skin-like surface points to surface tension. Rise in thin tubes points to capillarity.
patterns.why: Each principle has a small set of classic examples.

example.q: The roof of a hut is blown off in a storm. Which principle explains this?
steps: Fast wind moves over the roof.
Fast flow means low pressure above.
Higher pressure inside pushes the roof up.

patterns.name: Class of a lever
patterns.howToSpot: A tool (scissors, nutcracker, forceps, wheelbarrow, human arm) is given and 'lever of class ...' is asked.
steps: Find the fulcrum, load and effort on the tool.
See which one is in the middle.
Fulcrum gives class 1, load gives class 2, effort gives class 3.
patterns.why: The position of the middle item fixes the class.

example.q: A bottle opener is a lever of which class?
steps: The fulcrum is the edge on the cap top.
Your hand gives the effort at the far end.
The cap (load) is between them.

patterns.name: Work, energy and power basics
patterns.howToSpot: The question says 'If velocity is doubled, KE becomes ...', 'work done when ...', or asks a small power sum.
steps: KE depends on $v^2$. A speed multiplied by k gives KE multiplied by $k^2$.
Work is F × s × cos θ. It is zero if s = 0 or the force is perpendicular to motion.
Power is work ÷ time. For lifting, work is mgh.
patterns.why: The square in KE makes energy grow faster than speed.

example.q: A body's velocity is made three times. Its kinetic energy becomes:
steps: KE $\propto v^2$.

revision: Inertia measures mass. F = ma. Action equals reaction (rocket, recoil).
g is maximum at the poles, minimum at the equator and zero at the centre. Moon weight is about 1/6.
Escape velocity is 11.2 km/s. A geostationary satellite has a period of 24 h.
KE ∝ v². Work is zero if there is no displacement or the force is perpendicular to motion.
Pascal gives hydraulics. Archimedes gives floating. Bernoulli gives aeroplane lift.
Lever middle: fulcrum, load, effort gives class 1, 2, 3.

subtopics.title: Heat, temperature and sound
subtopics.concept: Heat is energy that flows from a hot body to a cold one. Temperature tells how hot a body is. Sound is a wave that needs a medium, and it travels fastest in solids. Exams ask temperature conversions, everyday heat effects and sound facts.

formulas.name: Latent heat
formulas.note: no temperature change during phase change

formulas.name: Echo distance
formulas.note: sound travels to the wall and back

tricks.title: Sound speed order
tricks.body: Solids are fastest, then liquids, then gases. A vacuum has no sound at all.

example.q: Why is an approaching train heard earlier through the rail?
steps: The rail is a solid.
Sound is faster in solids than in air.
example.answer: Sound travels much faster in steel than in air

example.q: The pitch of a sound depends on its:
steps: Pitch is how high or low a note is.
It follows the frequency.

mistakes.wrong: Thinking sound speed rises with pressure.
mistakes.right: It rises with temperature and humidity, not pressure alone.

mistakes.wrong: Calling the sound of bats infrasonic.
mistakes.right: Bats use ultrasonic sound, above 20 kHz.

mistakes.wrong: Saying the boiling point rises at hill stations.
mistakes.right: It falls, because the air pressure is lower.

mistakes.wrong: Using 'degree kelvin' or forgetting to add 273 for kelvin.
Thinking water is densest at 0 °C.
mistakes.right: Water is densest at 4 °C.

subtopics.notes:
### Heat and temperature are different
**Heat** is energy that flows from a hotter body to a colder one. Its unit is the joule. The older unit is the calorie.

**Temperature** tells how hot a body is. It is the average energy of its particles. Its unit is the kelvin.

A bucket of warm water holds more heat than a cup of boiling water. The cup has the higher temperature.

### Temperature scales
| Scale | Ice melts | Water boils |
|---|---|---|
| Celsius | 0 °C | 100 °C |
| Fahrenheit | 32 °F | 212 °F |
| Kelvin | 273 K (273.15) | 373 K |

The conversions are $F = \dfrac{9}{5}C + 32$ and $K = C + 273$.

- Celsius and Fahrenheit read the same at −40°.
- Normal body temperature is 37 °C = 98.6 °F = 310 K.
- The lowest possible temperature is 0 K, called absolute zero. It is −273.15 °C.
- A clinical thermometer reads about 35 to 42 °C. A pyrometer measures very high temperatures.

> **Example:** Convert 25 °C to °F. $\dfrac{9}{5} \times 25 + 32 = 45 + 32 = 77$ °F.

### Specific heat and latent heat
- **Specific heat** is the heat needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C. Water has a very high specific heat. It heats and cools slowly. So coastal places have mild climates, and water is used as a coolant.
- **Latent heat** is heat taken or given during a change of state, with no change in temperature. Steam at 100 °C burns more than water at 100 °C. Steam also gives out its latent heat of vaporisation when it condenses on skin.
- **Evaporation causes cooling.** A matka (earthen pot) keeps water cool. Sweat cools the body.

> **Tip:** Evaporation is faster with more surface area, more heat, wind and dry air.

### Boiling, melting and pressure
Higher pressure raises the boiling point. A pressure cooker cooks faster because water inside boils above 100 °C.

On mountains the air pressure is low. Water boils below 100 °C and food cooks slowly.

Pressure lowers the melting point of ice. This is called regelation. Two ice blocks pressed together join.

### Water expands the wrong way
Most things expand when heated. Water shrinks from 0 °C to 4 °C and then expands. So water is **densest at 4 °C**.

In winter the top of a lake freezes first. The floating ice insulates the water below, which stays near 4 °C. Fish survive.

Pipes burst in frost because water expands when it freezes. Gaps in railway tracks and sagging wires in summer show ordinary thermal expansion.

### Three ways heat travels
- **Conduction** moves heat through solids, particle to particle. A spoon handle gets hot this way. Metals conduct well. Wood, plastic and air are insulators.
- **Convection** moves heat when the liquid or gas itself moves. Examples are the sea breeze (day), the land breeze (night), boiling water and room heaters.
- **Radiation** needs no medium. The Sun's heat reaches us this way.

Dark, rough surfaces absorb and emit heat well. Light, shiny surfaces reflect it. So white clothes keep us cool in summer.

> **Note:** A thermos flask blocks all three. The vacuum stops conduction and convection. The silvered walls stop radiation.

### Sound is a mechanical wave
Sound comes from vibration. It is a **longitudinal wave** and it needs a medium. It cannot travel in a vacuum. Astronauts use radio.

| Medium | Speed of sound |
|---|---|
| Air at 0 °C | about 332 m/s |
| Air at 20 °C | about 343 m/s |
| Water | about 1500 m/s |
| Steel | about 5000 m/s or more |

The order is solids > liquids > gases. Speed rises with temperature and humidity. Pressure alone does not change it.

### Frequency, pitch and loudness
- Humans hear 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.
- Below 20 Hz is **infrasonic**: earthquakes, elephants, whales.
- Above 20 kHz is **ultrasonic**: bats, dolphins, SONAR, scans, cleaning.
- **Pitch** depends on frequency. Women and children have higher-pitched voices.
- **Loudness** depends on amplitude. It is measured in decibels (dB).
- **Quality (timbre)** depends on the wave shape. It lets us tell a sitar from a flute on the same note.

### Echo, Doppler effect and resonance
- **Echo:** a reflected sound is heard separately if it returns after at least 0.1 s. The reflector must be about 17 m away. Distance = speed × time ÷ 2.
- **Doppler effect:** an approaching horn sounds higher. A receding one sounds lower.
- **Resonance:** a body vibrates strongly when pushed at its natural frequency. Soldiers break step on a bridge.
- **Sonic boom:** made by objects that move faster than sound. Mach number is object speed ÷ speed of sound. Above 1 is supersonic.

patterns.name: Temperature scale conversion
patterns.howToSpot: A temperature must be converted, or the question asks when two scales read the same or one is double the other.
steps: Write $\dfrac{C}{5}=\dfrac{F-32}{9}$.
Put in the given value or the condition, such as F = C or F = 2C.
Solve for the unknown. For kelvin, just add 273.
patterns.why: 100 Celsius steps cover the same range as 180 Fahrenheit steps, so the ratio is 5 to 9 with a 32° shift.

example.q: Convert 25 °C to Fahrenheit.
steps: That is 45 + 32.

patterns.name: Everyday heat effect and its reason
patterns.howToSpot: The question says 'Why does steam burn more / pressure cooker cook faster / earthen pot cool water / fish survive frozen lakes / coast have mild climate?'
steps: A state change with no temperature change points to latent heat.
Slow heating or cooling of water points to high specific heat.
Boiling point rises with pressure and falls with height.
Cooling without a fridge points to evaporation. Lakes freezing from the top point to 4 °C density.
patterns.why: Each everyday effect has one standard reason.

example.q: Why does food take longer to cook on high mountains?
steps: Air pressure is low there.
Water boils below 100 °C.
The food gets less heat.
example.answer: Water boils at a lower temperature, so food cooks slowly

patterns.name: Mode of heat transfer
patterns.howToSpot: A situation (sea breeze, Sun's heat, hot spoon handle, thermos flask, white clothes) with conduction, convection and radiation as options.
steps: If heat moves through a solid and the solid stays still, choose conduction.
If the warm fluid itself moves (breezes, boiling), choose convection.
If no medium is needed, or colour matters, choose radiation.
patterns.why: The three modes differ in how the particles take part.

example.q: A land breeze at night is an example of:
steps: At night the sea is warmer.
Air over the sea rises.
Cooler air from the land moves in.

patterns.name: Speed of sound and the medium
patterns.howToSpot: The question says 'Sound travels fastest in ...', 'cannot travel through ...' or 'speed of sound increases with ...'.
steps: Recall the order: solids > liquids > gases. A vacuum has no sound.
Temperature and humidity raise the speed in air. Pressure alone does not.
Recall the values: air 343 m/s, water 1500 m/s, steel 5000 m/s.
patterns.why: Particles in a solid are closer, so the vibration passes faster.

example.q: In which medium is sound fastest: air, water, steel or vacuum?
steps: A vacuum has no sound.
Solids carry sound fastest.
Steel is a solid.

patterns.name: Frequency ranges, pitch, loudness and quality
patterns.howToSpot: The question gives the audible range, users of infrasonic or ultrasonic sound (bats, dolphins, elephants), or asks which property decides pitch, loudness or timbre.
steps: Audible range is 20 Hz to 20 kHz. Below it is infrasonic. Above it is ultrasonic.
Pitch goes with frequency. Loudness goes with amplitude (dB). Quality goes with the wave shape.
Ultrasound is used in SONAR, medical scans and bat echolocation.
patterns.why: Each property of the note is set by a different property of the wave.

example.q: Sound waves of frequency 10 Hz are called:
steps: The lower limit of hearing is 20 Hz.
10 Hz is below it.

patterns.name: Echo, Doppler effect and resonance
patterns.howToSpot: An echo-distance sum, a horn whose pitch rises as it approaches, or soldiers breaking step on a bridge.
steps: For echo, sound goes to the reflector and back. So distance = v × t ÷ 2.
If the heard pitch changes because source or listener moves, it is the Doppler effect.
If a body vibrates strongly at its natural frequency, it is resonance.
patterns.why: Echo time covers a round trip, so you halve it.

example.q: An echo returns in 3 s. The speed of sound is 330 m/s. How far is the wall?
steps: Round trip $= 330 \times 3 = 990$ m.
One way is 990 ÷ 2.

revision: F = 9C/5 + 32 and K = C + 273. −40 °C = −40 °F. Body temperature 37 °C = 98.6 °F.
Water has the highest specific heat and is densest at 4 °C.
Steam burns worse because of latent heat. A pressure cooker raises the boiling point.
Conduction: solids. Convection: fluids and breezes. Radiation: Sun, no medium needed.
Sound: solids fastest, no sound in vacuum, audible range 20 Hz to 20 kHz.
Pitch goes with frequency. Loudness goes with amplitude. Echo distance = vt/2.

subtopics.title: Light — mirrors, lenses, eye, dispersion and scattering
subtopics.concept: Light travels in straight lines at about 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum. Mirrors reflect it, lenses and glass bend it, and a prism splits it into colours. Exams ask which mirror or lens to use, eye defects, and why the sky is blue.

tricks.title: Eye defect and its lens
tricks.body: **My**opia goes with **con**cave. **Hyper**metropia goes with con**vex**. A short-sighted eye needs a diverging lens to push the image back onto the retina.

example.q: A person who cannot see distant objects clearly needs which lens?
steps: Cannot see far means short sight, or myopia.
Myopia goes with a concave lens.

tricks.title: Mirror by job
tricks.body: Need a wide view? Use convex (rear-view). Need an enlarged image or a focused beam? Use concave (shaving, dentist, headlight).

mistakes.wrong: Explaining the blue sky by reflection or refraction.
mistakes.right: The cause is scattering of short wavelengths.

mistakes.wrong: Saying red bends most in a prism.
mistakes.right: Violet bends most and red bends least.

mistakes.wrong: Choosing a concave mirror for a vehicle rear-view.
mistakes.right: Vehicles use convex mirrors for a wide view.

mistakes.wrong: Leaving the focal length in centimetres in P = 1/f.
mistakes.right: Convert to metres first: 25 cm = 0.25 m.

mistakes.wrong: Offering a lens as the cure for colour blindness.
mistakes.right: No lens can correct it.

subtopics.notes:
### Light, the basics
Light is a form of energy that makes things visible. In one medium it moves in straight lines. That is why shadows form.

- The speed of light in vacuum is $c \approx 3 \times 10^8$ m/s. It is the highest speed in the universe.
- Light slows down in water and glass.
- **Refractive index** is $n = \dfrac{c}{v}$. In glass, $n \approx 1.5$, so light moves at about $2 \times 10^8$ m/s.
- Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach the Earth.
- Diamond has a very high refractive index, about 2.42. It has a small critical angle, so it sparkles.

### Mirrors and their jobs
| Mirror | Image | Standard uses |
|---|---|---|
| Plane | Virtual, erect, same size, laterally inverted | Looking glass, periscope |
| Concave (converging) | Real and inverted if the object is far. Magnified virtual image if close. | Shaving and make-up mirror, dentist's mirror, headlight and torch reflectors, solar furnace |
| Convex (diverging) | Always virtual, erect, diminished. Wide field of view. | Rear-view mirror, mirrors at road bends |

A concave mirror brings parallel rays to a focus. So it collects the Sun's heat, or sends lamp light out as a beam.

> **Tip:** Need a wide view? Choose convex. Need an enlarged image or a beam? Choose concave.

### Lenses
A **convex lens** is thicker in the middle. It converges rays. It is used in a magnifier, camera, projector, microscope, telescope objective and the eye.

- Object inside F: image is magnified, erect and virtual (a magnifier).
- Object beyond 2F: image is real, inverted and diminished (a camera).

A **concave lens** always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image of a real object. It corrects short sight.

**Power** is $P = \dfrac{1}{f}$, with f in metres. The unit is the dioptre (D). Convex power is positive. Concave power is negative. For thin lenses in contact, powers simply add.

> **Example:** A lens of focal length 25 cm has $f = 0.25$ m. Its power is $\dfrac{1}{0.25} = +4$ D.

### The eye and its defects
The eye lens forms a real, inverted image on the retina. The brain reads it upright.

- Nearest clear vision is about 25 cm. The far point is at infinity.
- Rods work in dim light. Cones sense colour.
- Persistence of vision is about 1/16 s. It makes cinema possible.

| Defect | What goes wrong | Correction |
|---|---|---|
| Myopia (short sight) | Image forms in front of the retina | Concave lens |
| Hypermetropia (long sight) | Image forms behind the retina | Convex lens |
| Presbyopia | Old age, lens loses flexibility | Bifocal lens |
| Astigmatism | Uneven curve of the cornea | Cylindrical lens |
| Cataract | Lens turns opaque | Surgery |

Colour blindness is not a lens problem. The cones lack some colour sensors. No lens can correct it.

### Refraction and total internal reflection
Light bends when it passes at a slant between clear media. This is **refraction**. The speed changes. Light bends towards the normal in a denser medium.

- A pencil in water looks bent. A pool looks shallower.
- Stars twinkle because of shifting layers of air. Planets hardly twinkle.
- The Sun is seen about 2 minutes before actual sunrise and after actual sunset.

**Total internal reflection (TIR)** happens when light goes from a denser to a rarer medium beyond the critical angle. All the light reflects back. It gives the sparkle of a diamond, optical fibres, the endoscope and the mirage.

### Dispersion and scattering
White light is a mixture of seven colours, VIBGYOR. A prism splits it. This is **dispersion**. Violet bends most and red bends least. Newton recombined the colours with a second prism.

A **rainbow** forms by refraction, dispersion and internal reflection in raindrops. It is seen with the Sun behind you. In the primary rainbow, red is on the outside.

**Scattering** by air molecules is stronger for short wavelengths. So:
- The sky looks blue.
- The Sun looks red at sunrise and sunset.
- Danger signals are red, because red scatters least and is seen from far.
- The sky looks black to astronauts, because space has no air to scatter light.

> **Note:** The Raman effect was found by C.V. Raman on 28 February 1928. That day is National Science Day. He won the Nobel Prize in 1930.

Light primaries are red, green and blue. Red + green is yellow, green + blue is cyan, red + blue is magenta. All three make white. A red rose in green light looks almost black, because it reflects only red.

patterns.name: Mirror, image and use
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks which mirror is a rear-view, shaving or dentist's mirror, or which image a convex mirror forms, or plane mirror properties.
steps: Let the job decide. A wide upright view needs convex. An enlarged close view or a beam needs concave.
A convex mirror always gives a virtual, erect, diminished image.
A plane mirror image is virtual, erect, same size and laterally inverted.
patterns.why: Each mirror bends rays in a fixed way, so each has fixed jobs.

example.q: A dentist's mirror is a:
steps: The mirror is held close to the tooth.
The image must be erect and magnified.
Only a concave mirror does that.

patterns.name: Lens, image and use
patterns.howToSpot: The question says 'Which lens is used in a magnifier / camera / projector?', 'a concave lens always forms ...' or 'which lens converges light'.
steps: A converging lens is a convex lens: magnifier, camera, projector, eye lens.
A diverging lens is a concave lens. For real objects the image is virtual, erect and diminished.
For a magnifier, keep the object inside the focal length.
patterns.why: Convex lenses converge light. Concave lenses spread it out.

example.q: A camera lens produces an image that is:
steps: The object is far beyond 2F.
The image lands between F and 2F.
It is real, inverted and diminished.

patterns.name: Eye defects and correction
patterns.howToSpot: A defect (myopia, hypermetropia, presbyopia, astigmatism, cataract, colour blindness) is given with its cause or lens.
steps: Short-sighted is myopia, so choose a concave lens. Long-sighted is hypermetropia, so choose a convex lens.
Old-age trouble with near and far points to a bifocal lens. Uneven cornea points to a cylindrical lens. A cloudy lens is cataract, treated by surgery.
Colour blindness has no lens correction, so reject any lens option.
patterns.why: Each defect has one fixed cause and one fixed cure.

example.q: Presbyopia of old age is corrected by:
steps: Both near and far vision are weak.
One lens needs two parts.
Bifocal lenses have a convex lower part and a concave upper part.

patterns.name: Lens power and light-speed numericals
patterns.howToSpot: A focal length is given and power is asked (or the reverse), lenses are in contact, or a distance is divided by the speed of light.
steps: Convert the focal length to metres first.
Use P = 1/f. Convex is positive and concave is negative.
For lenses in contact, add the powers.
For light travel time, use t = d ÷ (3 × 10⁸ m/s).
patterns.why: The dioptre means 1 per metre, so the metre conversion is the only trap.

example.q: Two thin lenses of powers +2 D and −0.5 D are placed in contact. Find the power and nature of the combination.
steps: Add the powers: 2 + (−0.5) = 1.5.
The net power is positive.

patterns.name: Refraction and total internal reflection effects
patterns.howToSpot: A phenomenon (bent pencil, shallow pool, twinkling star, early sunrise, mirage, optical fibre, diamond sparkle) with its cause asked.
steps: If an object looks bent, shifted or shallow, or stars twinkle, or the Sun rises early, the cause is refraction.
If light stays inside (diamond, optical fibre, endoscope) or a mirage forms, the cause is total internal reflection.
TIR needs light going from a denser to a rarer medium beyond the critical angle.
patterns.why: Refraction comes from a change of speed between media.

example.q: Why do stars twinkle but planets hardly do?
steps: Starlight refracts through shifting layers of air.
So its brightness flickers.
Planets are closer and act as extended sources, so the changes average out.

patterns.name: Dispersion, scattering and colour facts
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks why the sky is blue, why danger signals are red, the VIBGYOR order, which colour bends most, rainbow facts, or an object's colour in coloured light.
steps: Blue sky, red sunset and red danger signals all come from scattering.
In a prism violet bends most and red bends least.
For a rainbow, remember dispersion plus internal reflection in raindrops, the Sun behind you, and red on the outer edge of the primary bow.
A body shows the colour it reflects. It looks black in light it fully absorbs.
patterns.why: Short wavelengths scatter most, and different colours bend by different amounts.

example.q: A red rose is seen in green light. What colour does it appear?
steps: The rose reflects only red light.
Green light has no red in it.
So the rose absorbs the green light.

revision: c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s. n = c/v. Sunlight takes about 8 min 20 s to reach Earth.
Plane mirror: lateral inversion. Concave: shaving, dentist, headlight. Convex: rear-view.
P = 1/f (metres) in dioptre. Powers add for lenses in contact.
Myopia: concave. Hypermetropia: convex. Presbyopia: bifocal. Astigmatism: cylindrical. Cataract: surgery.
TIR: diamond sparkle, optical fibre, mirage. Refraction: bent pencil, twinkling, early sunrise.
Violet bends most in a prism. Blue sky, red sunset and red danger signals come from scattering.

subtopics.title: Electricity, magnetism and the EM spectrum
subtopics.concept: Electric current is the flow of charge, pushed by voltage and opposed by resistance. Ohm's law, series and parallel circuits and the heating effect are the core numericals. Magnetism gives us the motor, generator and transformer. The electromagnetic spectrum is a fixed order of waves with fixed uses.

formulas.name: Ohm's law
formulas.note: V is voltage, I is current, R is resistance

formulas.name: Series resistance
formulas.note: the same current flows through each

tricks.title: Fleming's hands
tricks.body: **L** comes before **M**, so Left goes with Motor. **G** is for generator, so Right goes with Generator.

example.q: Which Fleming rule gives the direction of the force in an electric motor?
steps: The motor uses a force on a current-carrying wire.
Left for Motor.

tricks.title: Spectrum order
tricks.body: **G**ood **X**-rays **U**se **V**isible **I**nfra-**M**icro **R**adios. The wavelength rises along the list. Frequency and energy fall.

example.q: Which has the longest wavelength: X-rays, UV, microwaves or gamma rays?
steps: Order by rising wavelength: gamma, X-ray, UV, microwave.
The last one is the longest.

mistakes.wrong: Thinking a fuse wire should have a high melting point.
mistakes.right: It must melt easily, so use a low-melting alloy.

mistakes.wrong: Saying a transformer works on DC.
mistakes.right: It needs changing current, so it works only on AC.

mistakes.wrong: Connecting an ammeter in parallel.
mistakes.right: An ammeter goes in series. A voltmeter goes in parallel.

subtopics.notes:
### Current, voltage and resistance
**Electric current** is the flow of charge. $I = \dfrac{Q}{t}$ and its unit is the ampere (A).

A **potential difference** (voltage) pushes the charges. Its unit is the volt (V). A voltmeter measures it.

**Resistance** is the wire's opposition to the flow. Its unit is the ohm (Ω).

**Ohm's law** says $V = IR$ at constant temperature. Double the voltage and the current doubles.

Resistance is $R = \rho\dfrac{L}{A}$. More length means more resistance. A thicker wire means less. It also depends on the material (resistivity ρ) and on temperature. Metals conduct best. Rubber, plastic and mica are insulators.

### Series and parallel circuits
| | Series | Parallel |
|---|---|---|
| Layout | One loop | Branches across two points |
| Common to all | Current | Voltage |
| Total resistance | $R = R_1 + R_2 + \cdots$ | $\dfrac{1}{R} = \dfrac{1}{R_1} + \dfrac{1}{R_2} + \cdots$ |
| If one bulb fuses | All go dark | Others keep working |

In parallel, the total resistance is less than the smallest branch. Homes are wired in parallel. Each appliance gets the full 220 V and works independently.

> **Example:** 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 6 Ω in parallel: $\dfrac{1}{R} = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{6} = 1$. So $R = 1$ Ω.

### Power, energy and heating
Power is $P = VI = I^2R = \dfrac{V^2}{R}$. Its unit is the watt. A 100 W bulb at 220 V draws about 0.45 A.

Electricity is sold in kilowatt-hours. 1 unit = 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. Units = watts × hours ÷ 1000.

**Joule's law** says $H = I^2Rt$. Heat grows with current squared, resistance and time. Irons, geysers and heaters work this way.

- The bulb **filament** is tungsten. It has a very high melting point.
- Heating coils are **nichrome**. It has high resistivity.
- A **fuse** wire is a tin–lead alloy with a low melting point. It melts on excess current. It sits in series with the live wire.

### Household supply
Indian domestic supply is AC at about 220 V (220–230 V) and 50 Hz.

| Wire | Colour |
|---|---|
| Live | Red or brown |
| Neutral | Black or blue |
| Earth | Green |

The earth wire gives a safe path to the ground for metal bodies.

### Magnetism and its devices
A magnet has north and south poles. Like poles repel and unlike poles attract.

- **Oersted (1820):** a current in a wire deflects a compass. Electricity creates magnetism.
- **Electromagnet:** a coil with a soft-iron core. It is temporary. Cranes and bells use it. Steel makes permanent magnets.
- **Faraday (1831):** a changing magnetic field induces a current. This is electromagnetic induction. It runs the generator or dynamo.
- **Electric motor:** current plus a magnetic field gives rotation.
- **Transformer:** changes AC voltage by mutual induction. It works only on AC. Step-up transformers raise voltage for long-distance lines. The current falls, so the I²R loss falls. Step-down transformers lower it near homes.

> **Rule:** Fleming's left-hand rule is for the motor. The right-hand rule is for the generator. Remember "L for Motor, R for Generator".

A galvanometer becomes an **ammeter** with a low-resistance shunt in parallel. An ammeter is connected in series. A **voltmeter** has a high resistance in series inside it. It is connected in parallel.

### AC, DC and semiconductors
**AC** reverses direction again and again (mains supply). **DC** flows one way (cells, batteries).

- A **rectifier (diode)** turns AC into DC. An **inverter** turns DC into AC.
- The **transistor** (1947, Bell Labs) amplifies and switches signals.
- **Semiconductors** are silicon and germanium. They conduct between metals and insulators.
- A **pentavalent** impurity (phosphorus, arsenic) adds free electrons. That gives **n-type**.
- A **trivalent** impurity (boron, gallium) leaves holes. That gives **p-type**.

### The electromagnetic spectrum
EM waves need no medium. They travel at $c = 3 \times 10^8$ m/s in vacuum. In order of increasing wavelength:

**Gamma rays, X-rays, Ultraviolet, Visible, Infrared, Microwaves, Radio waves.**

| Wave | Use |
|---|---|
| Gamma | Cancer treatment, sterilising tools |
| X-rays | Bone imaging, airport scanners |
| Ultraviolet | Sterilisation, vitamin D in skin |
| Visible | Seeing, lasers |
| Infrared | TV remotes, night vision, heaters |
| Microwaves | Microwave ovens, radar, satellite links |
| Radio | Broadcasting, mobile phones |

patterns.name: Ohm's law and series or parallel circuits
patterns.howToSpot: The question gives two or three resistors and asks total resistance, gives voltage and resistance and asks current, or asks what stays the same in series or parallel.
steps: In series, add the resistances. The current is common.
In parallel, add the reciprocals, then invert. For two resistors use R₁R₂/(R₁+R₂).
Three equal resistors R in parallel give R/3.
For current, use I = V/R.
patterns.why: One path shares current (series). Branches share voltage (parallel).

example.q: Resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 6 Ω are joined in parallel. Find the total resistance.
steps: So R = 1 Ω, less than the smallest resistor.

patterns.name: Power, kWh and the heating effect
patterns.howToSpot: The question gives appliance watts and hours, H = I²Rt, 'the filament is made of ...', 'why is the fuse wire low-melting', or transmission steps.
steps: For energy, use kW × hours = units. Multiply by the tariff for rupees.
For heat, use H = I²Rt with t in seconds.
Filament is tungsten. Coil is nichrome. Fuse is a low-melting alloy in series with the live wire.
Long lines run at high voltage so the current and I²R loss stay small.
patterns.why: Watts times hours gives energy. Current squared gives heat.

example.q: A 2 kW heater runs for 3 hours. How many units does it use?
steps: Units = kW × hours.

patterns.name: Electricity and magnetism devices
patterns.howToSpot: The question says 'The electric motor works on ...', 'a generator is based on ...', 'a transformer works on ...', asks which Fleming rule applies, or who found electromagnetic induction.
steps: Oersted: a current makes a magnetic field.
Motor: a magnetic force on a current-carrying wire. Use the left-hand rule.
Generator: electromagnetic induction (Faraday). Use the right-hand rule.
Transformer: mutual induction. AC only. Step-up raises V and lowers I.
patterns.why: Each device turns one effect of electricity or magnetism into work.

example.q: The working of an electric motor is based on:
steps: A wire carries current inside a magnetic field.
The field pushes the wire.
The left-hand rule gives the direction.
example.answer: The magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor

patterns.name: Household wiring and safety
patterns.howToSpot: The question says 'Appliances in a house are connected in ...', asks the colour of the earth wire, the job of the fuse, or mains voltage and frequency in India.
steps: Homes use parallel wiring. Each appliance gets full voltage and has its own switch.
Live is red or brown. Neutral is black. Earth is green.
The fuse is low-melting and sits in series with the live wire. It melts first on overload.
India uses AC at about 220 V and 50 Hz.
patterns.why: The wiring plan protects both the appliance and the person.

example.q: Which colour of insulation is used for the earth wire in India?
steps: Live is red or brown.
Neutral is black.
Earth is the remaining one.

patterns.name: EM spectrum order and uses
patterns.howToSpot: The question says 'Arrange gamma to radio by wavelength', 'TV remote uses ...', 'which wave is used in radar / microwave oven' or 'UV makes which vitamin'.
steps: Learn rising wavelength: gamma, X, UV, visible, IR, microwave, radio. Frequency runs the other way.
Match uses: gamma for cancer therapy, X-ray for bones, UV for sterilising and vitamin D, IR for remotes, microwave for ovens and radar, radio for broadcast.
All EM waves travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum and need no medium.
patterns.why: The order and the uses are fixed facts.

example.q: Which electromagnetic wave is used in TV remotes?
steps: Remotes send invisible beams.
They lie just beyond the red end of visible light.

patterns.name: Semiconductors, rectifiers and electronics
patterns.howToSpot: The question says 'n-type is doped with ...', 'which device converts AC to DC', or asks about transistors and semiconductor materials.
steps: Semiconductors are silicon and germanium.
Pentavalent doping (P, As) gives n-type, with extra electrons. Trivalent doping (B, Ga) gives p-type, with holes.
A diode is a rectifier (AC to DC). An inverter changes DC to AC. The transistor (1947) amplifies and switches.
patterns.why: The number of outer electrons in the impurity decides n-type or p-type.

example.q: A pure silicon crystal doped with a pentavalent impurity such as phosphorus becomes:
steps: Phosphorus has one extra outer electron.
It gives a free electron to the crystal.
Free electrons are negative carriers.

revision: I = Q/t and V = IR. R = ρL/A: longer means more, thicker means less.
Series: same current, resistances add. Parallel: same voltage, total R is smaller. Homes are parallel.
P = VI. 1 unit = 1 kWh. H = I²Rt. Filament is tungsten, coil is nichrome, fuse is low-melting in the live wire.
Oersted: current gives magnetism. Faraday, 1831: induction gives the generator. Left hand for motor, right for generator.
A transformer works on AC only. Step-up is used for transmission. A rectifier turns AC to DC. The transistor is from 1947.
EM waves by rising wavelength: gamma, X, UV, visible, IR, microwave, radio.

subtopics.title: Nuclear physics, inventions and scientists
subtopics.concept: The atom has a nucleus of protons and neutrons with electrons around it. Radioactivity, fission and fusion come from the nucleus. Exams ask who found what, which invention belongs to whom, and India's nuclear and space firsts.

tricks.title: Fission or fusion
tricks.body: **Fission** means split: heavy nucleus to lighter ones (reactors, atom bomb). **Fusion** means join: light nuclei to a heavier one (Sun, hydrogen bomb).

example.q: The energy of the Sun comes from:
steps: The Sun is made mostly of hydrogen.
Hydrogen nuclei join into helium.
Joining is fusion.

tricks.title: Particle discoverers
tricks.body: Electron: **T**homson (1897). Nucleus: **R**utherford. Neutron: **Chad**wick (1932). Proton rays: Goldstein.

mistakes.wrong: Saying Einstein won the Nobel Prize for relativity.
mistakes.right: It was for the photoelectric effect (1921).

mistakes.wrong: Saying the moderator absorbs neutrons.
mistakes.right: The moderator slows them. Control rods (cadmium, boron) absorb them.

mistakes.wrong: Crediting Edison with the telephone.
mistakes.right: The telephone was Alexander Graham Bell's. Edison made the bulb and phonograph.

mistakes.wrong: Saying a reactor uses fusion.
mistakes.right: Reactors use fission. Fusion powers the Sun and the hydrogen bomb.

mistakes.wrong: Taking gamma rays as particles.
mistakes.right: Gamma rays are electromagnetic waves, the most penetrating of the three.

subtopics.notes:
### Inside the atom
An atom has a tiny, dense **nucleus** of protons and neutrons. Electrons move around it.

- **Electron:** negative charge. Found by J.J. Thomson (1897) in cathode-ray experiments.
- **Proton:** positive charge. Seen in canal rays by E. Goldstein.
- **Neutron:** no charge. Discovered by James Chadwick (1932).
- **Nucleus:** shown by Rutherford's gold-foil experiment (1911). Most alpha particles went straight through and a few bounced back. So nearly all the mass and positive charge sit in a tiny centre.
- **Bohr (1913):** added fixed orbits for electrons.

### Radioactivity
**Henri Becquerel (1896)** found that uranium salts give out invisible, penetrating rays. This is radioactivity. It belongs to heavy, unstable nuclei.

**Marie and Pierre Curie** discovered polonium and radium. Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in Physics (1903) and Chemistry (1911).

| Ray | What it is | Penetration |
|---|---|---|
| Alpha | Helium nucleus | Least. Paper stops it. |
| Beta | Fast electron | Medium. Aluminium stops it. |
| Gamma | Electromagnetic wave | Most. Thick lead needed. |

A **Geiger–Müller counter** detects radiation. **Willard Libby's carbon-14 dating** finds the age of old organic remains.

### Fission, fusion and reactors
- **Fission:** a heavy nucleus such as U-235 splits when a neutron hits it. It releases energy and more neutrons. That is a chain reaction. Uncontrolled, it is the atom bomb (Hiroshima, 1945). Controlled, it makes electricity.
- **Fusion:** light nuclei (hydrogen isotopes) join into a heavier one. It powers the Sun and stars, and the hydrogen bomb.
- Both follow Einstein's $E = mc^2$. A little lost mass becomes a lot of energy.

> **Rule:** Fission means split. Fusion means join. Reactors use fission, not fusion.

In a reactor, the **moderator** (heavy water, graphite) slows neutrons. **Control rods** (cadmium, boron) absorb neutrons. A coolant carries the heat away.

### India's atomic and space firsts
**Homi J. Bhabha** is the father of India's nuclear programme. He set up the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (1945) and BARC at Trombay.

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| Apsara (1956) | First research reactor in Asia |
| Tarapur (1969) | First nuclear power station, Maharashtra |
| Pokhran-I (1974) | First nuclear test, "Smiling Buddha" |
| Pokhran-II | May 1998 |
| ISRO | Formed in 1969 |
| Aryabhata (1975) | First Indian satellite |
| Chandrayaan-1 (2008) | Found water molecules on the Moon |
| Mangalyaan (2013) | Reached Mars orbit at the first attempt |
| Chandrayaan-3 (23 Aug 2023) | First soft landing near the Moon's south pole |
| Aditya-L1 (2023) | India's first solar mission |

**Vikram Sarabhai** is the father of India's space programme. 23 August is now National Space Day. **Rakesh Sharma (1984)** was the first Indian in space. **Shubhanshu Shukla (2025, Axiom-4)** was the first Indian to visit the International Space Station.

### Inventions and who made them
| Invention or discovery | Person |
|---|---|
| Laws of motion, gravitation | Isaac Newton |
| Astronomical telescope | Galileo Galilei |
| Barometer | Evangelista Torricelli |
| Improved steam engine | James Watt |
| Electromagnetic induction, dynamo | Michael Faraday |
| Telephone | Alexander Graham Bell |
| Electric bulb, phonograph | Thomas Edison |
| Radio (wireless) | Guglielmo Marconi |
| Television | John Logie Baird |
| Telegraph | Samuel Morse |
| Aeroplane (1903) | Wright brothers |
| X-rays | Wilhelm Röntgen (first Physics Nobel, 1901) |
| Laser (1960) | Theodore Maiman |
| Dynamite | Alfred Nobel |
| Crescograph | J.C. Bose |
