Einstein gave the theory of relativity. His Nobel Prize (1921) was for the photoelectric effect.

A **laser** gives an intense beam of one wavelength, in step (coherent). It is used in surgery, barcode scanners, CD/DVD players and optical-fibre communication. At CERN's Large Hadron Collider (2012), scientists found the **Higgs boson**, the "God particle". It explains why other particles have mass.

patterns.name: Particle or ray and its discoverer
patterns.howToSpot: The question says 'Who discovered the neutron / electron / proton / X-rays / radioactivity / nucleus?' or gives a match-the-column.
steps: Particles: electron by J.J. Thomson, proton by Goldstein, neutron by Chadwick, nucleus by Rutherford.
Rays: X-rays by Röntgen, radioactivity by Becquerel, radium by the Curies.
Models: gold-foil experiment by Rutherford, orbits by Bohr.
patterns.why: Each name is fixed by history, so only recall and elimination work.

example.q: The canal rays that led to the discovery of the proton were observed by:
steps: Thomson found the electron in cathode rays.
Chadwick found the neutron in 1932.
Canal rays belong to Goldstein.

patterns.name: Device and its inventor
patterns.howToSpot: The question says 'Who invented the telephone / television / radio / electric bulb / dynamo / steam engine / aeroplane?'
steps: Bell made the telephone. Baird made television. Marconi made radio. Edison made the bulb and phonograph. Morse made the telegraph.
Faraday found induction and the dynamo. Watt improved the steam engine. The Wright brothers built the aeroplane (1903). Galileo used the astronomical telescope. Torricelli made the barometer.
Drop near-names. J.C. Bose did pioneering microwave work, but the exam answer for radio is Marconi.
patterns.why: Inventions are fixed facts, so match each device to one name.

example.q: The television was invented by:
steps: Telephone is Bell.
Radio is Marconi.
Television is Baird.

patterns.name: Radioactivity and alpha, beta, gamma
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks 'Which radiation is most penetrating?', 'an alpha particle is ...', who found radioactivity, or which instrument detects radiation.
steps: Radioactivity: Becquerel (1896). Radium and polonium: the Curies.
Alpha is a helium nucleus of 2 protons and 2 neutrons. Paper stops it. Beta is a fast electron. Gamma is an EM wave and the most penetrating.
The Geiger–Müller counter detects radiation. Libby's C-14 dating ages old remains.
patterns.why: The three rays differ in what they are and how far they go.

example.q: An alpha particle is identical to:
steps: An alpha particle has 2 protons and 2 neutrons.
That is the makeup of helium-4.
It has no electrons.

patterns.name: Fission or fusion; reactor parts
patterns.howToSpot: The question says 'The Sun's energy comes from ...', 'an atom bomb works on ...', 'control rods are made of ...', or compares the two bombs.
steps: If a heavy nucleus splits, it is fission (reactors, atom bomb).
If light nuclei join, it is fusion (Sun and stars, hydrogen bomb).
Moderator slows neutrons (heavy water, graphite). Control rods absorb them (cadmium, boron). A coolant removes heat.
patterns.why: Both follow E = mc². The size of the nuclei tells you which process it is.

example.q: The energy of the Sun and stars is due to:
steps: Stars are mostly hydrogen.
Hydrogen nuclei join into helium.
This releases energy through E = mc².

patterns.name: India's atomic and space milestones
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks for the first reactor, power station, satellite, Mars or Moon mission, the fathers of the two programmes, Pokhran tests or National Space Day.
steps: Atomic: Bhabha is the father. Apsara 1956 was the first research reactor. Tarapur 1969 was the first power station. Pokhran tests were 1974 and 1998.
Space: Sarabhai is the father. ISRO 1969. Aryabhata 1975. Chandrayaan-1 2008. Mangalyaan 2013. Chandrayaan-3 landed on 23 Aug 2023. Aditya-L1 is the solar mission.
Rakesh Sharma was the first Indian in space (1984). Shubhanshu Shukla was the first Indian on the ISS (2025).
patterns.why: Each milestone is a fixed name, place or date.

example.q: India's first nuclear power station was set up at:
steps: Apsara was a research reactor, at Trombay (1956).
A power station came later, in 1969.

patterns.name: Modern physics miscellany
patterns.howToSpot: One-line fact questions on E = mc², the 'God particle', laser properties, carbon dating or first Nobel Prizes.
steps: E = mc² is Einstein's. Mass can turn into energy. It is the base of fission and fusion.
The Higgs boson (the 'God particle') was found at CERN's LHC in 2012.
Laser light has one wavelength, is coherent and is highly directional.
Carbon-14 dating is Libby's method for fossils and old organic objects.
patterns.why: Each fact is a short, fixed statement.

example.q: The 'God particle' whose existence was confirmed at CERN in 2012 is the:
steps: It explains why particles have mass.
It was predicted by Peter Higgs.

revision: Electron: Thomson. Proton: Goldstein (canal rays). Neutron: Chadwick. Nucleus: Rutherford. Orbits: Bohr.
Radioactivity: Becquerel. Radium and polonium: the Curies. C-14 dating: Libby. Counter: Geiger.
Alpha is a helium nucleus. Beta is an electron. Gamma is an EM wave and the most penetrating.
Fission is heavy splitting (reactor, atom bomb). Fusion is light joining (Sun, H-bomb). E = mc².
Bhabha is atomic, Sarabhai is space. Apsara 1956, Tarapur 1969, Pokhran 1974 and 1998.
Aryabhata 1975. Chandrayaan-3 landed on 23 Aug 2023. Mangalyaan reached Mars orbit at the first attempt.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "The SI unit of magnetic flux / pressure / power is..."
pyqPatterns.approach:
Learn the unit names: newton = force, joule = energy, watt = power, pascal = pressure, hertz = frequency.
Weber = magnetic flux, tesla = magnetic field. Light year is distance; kWh is energy.

example.q: What is the SI unit of magnetic flux?
example.solution:
Magnetic flux = field × area
Its unit is the weber (Wb)
Tesla is the unit of magnetic field, not flux
**Weber**

pyqPatterns.approach: Use the root word: hygro = moisture, baro = pressure, anemo = wind, seismo = earthquake, lacto = milk.

example.q: Which instrument measures the humidity of air?
example.solution:
"Hygro" means moisture
So the instrument measures moisture in air
It is the hygrometer
**Hygrometer**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A daily-life effect (rocket, hydraulic brakes, floating ship) is given, with laws as options.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Match the story to the law.
Rocket or gun recoil = Newton's third law; enclosed liquid = Pascal; floating = Archimedes; fast air, low pressure = Bernoulli.

example.q: Hydraulic brakes work on which principle?
example.solution:
Brake fluid is enclosed in pipes
Pressure added at one end spreads equally in the liquid
A small push on the pedal gives a big force at the brakes
This is **Pascal's law**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "Who discovered the neutron?" or "who invented the telephone?"
pyqPatterns.approach:
Electron = Thomson, proton = Goldstein, neutron = Chadwick, nucleus = Rutherford, X-rays = Röntgen.
Telephone = Bell, radio = Marconi, bulb = Edison, TV = Baird.

example.q: Who discovered the neutron?
example.solution:
The neutron is a particle with no charge
It sits in the nucleus
It was found in 1932 by Chadwick
**James Chadwick**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "Myopia is corrected by..." or "which mirror is used as a rear-view mirror?"
pyqPatterns.approach:
Myopia = concave lens. Hypermetropia = convex lens.
Rear-view mirror is convex. Shaving mirror and torch use a concave mirror.

example.q: Myopia (short-sightedness) is corrected by which lens?
example.solution:
In myopia the image forms in front of the retina
A diverging lens pushes it back onto the retina
A diverging lens is a concave lens
**Concave lens**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A one-step sum: lens power, parallel resistors, units of electricity, or speed conversion.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Lens power P = 1/f (f in metres). Parallel resistors: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂.
kWh = watts × hours ÷ 1000. To change km/h to m/s, multiply by 5/18.

example.q: Two resistors of 6 Ω and 3 Ω are joined in parallel. Find the equivalent resistance.
example.solution:
1/R = 1/6 + 1/3
= 1/6 + 2/6 = 3/6 = 1/2
So R = 2
The equivalent resistance is **2 Ω**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "Sound cannot travel through..." or "pitch depends on..."
pyqPatterns.approach:
Sound needs a medium and cannot travel in a vacuum.
Pitch depends on frequency; loudness depends on amplitude. Audible range is 20 Hz to 20 kHz.

example.q: The pitch of a sound depends on its what?
example.solution:
A higher frequency gives a shriller sound
So pitch follows frequency
Amplitude decides loudness, not pitch
**Frequency**

solvedExamples.q: Which of the following is the SI unit of luminous intensity?
solvedExamples.solution: **Candela** is one of the 7 SI **base** units and measures luminous intensity. The **lumen** is luminous flux and the **lux** is illuminance (lumen per square metre); the watt is power.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Of the three light units only candela is a base unit — 'Mighty Kings … Correctly' ends with C.

solvedExamples.q: What is the power of a convex lens of focal length 50 cm?
solvedExamples.solution: P = 1/f with f in metres. f = 50 cm = 0.5 m, so P = 1/0.5 = **+2 D**. The sign is positive because a convex lens is converging.

solvedExamples.q: The sky appears blue because of:
options: Reflection of light by the ocean
Refraction of light by the atmosphere
Scattering of light by air molecules
solvedExamples.solution: Air molecules scatter shorter wavelengths far more than longer ones (**Rayleigh scattering**, ∝ 1/λ⁴). Blue light is scattered all over the sky, so it looks blue. The same effect makes the rising and setting Sun look red.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Colour of the sky/sunset/danger signal → always scattering.

solvedExamples.q: At what temperature do the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales show the same reading?
solvedExamples.shortcut: Memorise: −40 is the only common reading.

practice.q: A light year is a unit of:
practice.solution: A **light year** is the **distance** light travels in one year — about **9.46 × 10¹⁵ m**. It is used for astronomical distances, not time.

practice.q: Which instrument is used to measure the relative humidity of air?
practice.solution: A **hygrometer** measures humidity. A hydrometer measures the relative density of liquids, a barometer measures atmospheric pressure and an anemometer measures wind speed.

practice.q: The SI unit of magnetic flux is:
practice.solution: Magnetic **flux** is measured in **weber (Wb)**. **Tesla** is the unit of magnetic field (flux density), **henry** is inductance and **gauss** is a CGS unit of field.

practice.q: A 100 W bulb glows for 10 hours. How much electrical energy does it consume?
practice.solution: Energy = power × time = 100 W × 10 h = 1,000 Wh = **1 kWh** (1 unit).

practice.q: The recoil of a gun when a bullet is fired is an example of:
options: Newton's third law / conservation of momentum
practice.solution: The bullet is pushed forward and the gun is pushed back with an equal and opposite force (**third law**). Equivalently, the total momentum of gun + bullet stays zero (**conservation of momentum**).

practice.q: Hydraulic brakes in vehicles work on the principle of:
practice.solution: **Pascal's law**: pressure applied to an enclosed incompressible fluid is transmitted equally in all directions. Hydraulic brakes, lifts and presses use it.

practice.q: The value of acceleration due to gravity (g) on the Earth's surface is:
options: Maximum at the Tropic of Cancer
practice.solution: The Earth is slightly flattened at the poles, so the poles are closer to the centre, and there is no rotational effect there. Hence **g is maximum at the poles** and minimum at the equator.

practice.q: A nutcracker is an example of which class of lever?
practice.solution: In a nutcracker the **load (nut) lies between** the hinge (fulcrum) and the hands (effort), making it a **class 2** lever, like a wheelbarrow and a bottle opener.

practice.q: Why do steam burns cause more severe injuries than boiling water at the same temperature?
options: Steam is at a higher pressure
Steam releases extra latent heat when it condenses
practice.solution: Steam at 100 °C gives out its **latent heat of vaporisation** (about 2,260 J per gram) as it condenses on skin, in addition to the heat released by cooling. Boiling water gives only the cooling heat.

practice.q: Bats navigate in the dark using:
practice.solution: Bats emit **ultrasonic** sounds (above 20 kHz) and locate obstacles and prey from the echoes — **echolocation**, the same idea as SONAR.

practice.q: Sound cannot travel through:
practice.solution: Sound is a mechanical wave and needs a **material medium**. It travels fastest in solids, then liquids, then gases, and **not at all in a vacuum**.

practice.q: Myopia (short-sightedness) is corrected by using a:
practice.solution: In **myopia** the image of a distant object forms **in front of the retina**. A **concave (diverging) lens** spreads the rays so the image moves back onto the retina.

practice.q: The sparkling of a diamond is mainly due to:
practice.solution: Diamond's high refractive index (about 2.42) gives it a small critical angle (about 24°), so light entering it undergoes repeated **total internal reflection** before emerging — making it sparkle.

practice.q: Two resistors of 6 Ω and 3 Ω are connected in parallel. What is their equivalent resistance?
practice.solution: For two resistors in parallel, R = R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂) = (6 × 3)/(6 + 3) = 18/9 = **2 Ω**.
practice.shortcut: Parallel result is always smaller than the smallest resistor (3 Ω) — only 2 Ω or 0.5 Ω qualify; product/sum gives 2.

practice.q: Who discovered the neutron?
practice.solution: **James Chadwick** discovered the neutron in **1932** (Nobel Prize 1935). Thomson discovered the electron and Rutherford the atomic nucleus.
practice.shortcut: 'Tom Ran Chasing' — the third particle goes to Chadwick.

practice.q: The SI unit of **pressure** is —
practice.solution: Pressure = force ÷ area, so its SI unit is N/m², named **pascal (Pa)**. Bar and atmosphere are practical units; newton is the unit of force.

practice.q: The SI unit of **electric charge** is —
practice.solution: Charge is measured in **coulomb (C)**; 1 C = 1 ampere × 1 second. Ampere is current, volt is potential difference, farad is capacitance.

practice.q: Which pair of quantity and SI unit is **wrongly** matched?
practice.solution: Momentum = mass × velocity, so its unit is **kg·m/s**. Newton is the unit of force. The other three pairs are correct.
practice.shortcut: Momentum has no named unit — any 'named' answer for it is wrong.

practice.q: The instrument used to measure **blood pressure** is —
practice.solution: A **sphygmomanometer** (sphygmo = pulse) measures blood pressure, usually in mm of mercury. A manometer measures gas pressure, a barometer air pressure; a stethoscope only lets the doctor hear sounds.

practice.q: An **anemometer** measures —
practice.solution: **Anemo** means wind. The anemometer (rotating cups) measures wind speed. Pressure = barometer, humidity = hygrometer, height = altimeter.

practice.q: A **lactometer** is used to test —
practice.solution: A lactometer is a special hydrometer. It measures the **density (specific gravity) of milk**; watered milk has a lower density, so the lactometer shows adulteration.

practice.q: Which instrument records the waves produced by an **earthquake**?
practice.solution: A **seismograph** records ground shaking. Pyrometer = very high temperature, tachometer = rpm of an engine, altimeter = altitude.

practice.q: One **nautical mile** is equal to —
practice.solution: A nautical mile is **1852 m**, used at sea and in the air. 1609 m is the ordinary (statute) mile; 1760 is the number of yards in a mile.

practice.q: **Knot** is a unit of —
practice.solution: 1 knot = 1 nautical mile per hour (≈ 1.852 km/h). It is a unit of **speed**. Depth of the sea uses the fathom; purity of gold uses carat.

practice.q: One **horsepower** is approximately equal to —
practice.solution: 1 horsepower ≈ **746 watt**. (550 is the value in foot-pounds per second, a common trap.)

practice.q: Which of the following is **NOT** one of the seven SI base units?
practice.solution: The base units are metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela. The **newton** is derived: 1 N = 1 kg·m/s².
practice.shortcut: Named after a person but not in the 7-list = derived (only kelvin and ampere are both).

practice.q: Which of the following is a **vector** quantity?
practice.solution: **Velocity** is speed in a stated direction, so it is a vector. Speed, mass and energy have only magnitude — scalars.

practice.q: A train runs at **72 km/h**. Its speed in m/s is —
practice.solution: 72 × 5/18 = **20 m/s**. Multiplying by 3.6 instead (259.2) is the reverse conversion and a common mistake.

practice.q: A **1500 W** geyser runs 2 hours a day for 30 days. At ₹6 per unit, the electricity cost is —
Passengers standing in a moving bus fall **forward** when the driver brakes suddenly. This is due to —
practice.solution: The feet stop with the bus, but the upper body keeps moving forward because of **inertia of motion** (Newton's first law).

practice.q: A cricketer pulls his hands backward while catching a fast ball in order to —
options: Increase the time of impact and so reduce the force
Increase the momentum of the ball
Increase the force on the ball
practice.solution: Force = change in momentum ÷ time. The ball's momentum must fall to zero anyway; taking **more time** makes the force on the palms **smaller** (Newton's second law).
practice.shortcut: Same idea: air bags, crumple zones, sand in a long-jump pit.

practice.q: The upward motion of a **rocket** is based on —
practice.solution: The rocket pushes hot gases **downward** (action); the gases push the rocket **upward** (reaction) — Newton's third law, also seen as conservation of momentum.

practice.q: A man weighs **600 N** on the Earth. His weight on the Moon will be about —
practice.solution: g on the Moon is about **1/6** of Earth's, so weight ≈ 600 ÷ 6 = **100 N**. His **mass** stays the same.

practice.q: The **escape velocity** from the Earth's surface is about —
practice.solution: An object must be launched at about **11.2 km/s** to escape Earth's gravity. 7.9 km/s is the orbital speed just above the surface.

practice.q: The acceleration due to gravity (g) at the **centre of the Earth** is —
practice.solution: g falls as we go deeper, because less mass lies 'below' us. At the centre the pull from all sides cancels and **g = 0**.
practice.shortcut: g is zero at the centre, largest at the poles.

practice.q: A **geostationary satellite** completes one orbit round the Earth in —
practice.solution: It orbits above the equator at about 36,000 km, taking **24 hours** — the same as Earth's rotation — so it looks fixed from the ground. 90 minutes is typical of low-orbit satellites; 27 days is roughly the Moon's orbit.

practice.q: A ship made of steel floats on water because of —
practice.solution: The hollow ship displaces a large volume of water; the upthrust (weight of displaced water) equals the ship's weight — **Archimedes' principle**.

practice.q: The upward **lift** on the wings of an aeroplane is explained by —
practice.solution: Air flows faster over the curved upper surface of the wing, so pressure there is lower than below — the pressure difference lifts the plane (**Bernoulli**).

practice.q: Oil rises up the wick of a lamp because of —
practice.solution: The wick has many fine channels that act like thin tubes; oil climbs them by **capillarity**. Blotting paper works the same way.

practice.q: The **human forearm** lifting a weight works as a lever of —
practice.solution: Elbow = fulcrum, weight in the hand = load, biceps pull between them = effort. Effort in the middle → **class 3**.

practice.q: Which of the following is a **Class 2** lever?
practice.solution: In a **wheelbarrow** the wheel is the fulcrum, the load sits in the middle, and effort is at the handles — class 2. Seesaw is class 1; fishing rod and forceps are class 3.

practice.q: If the speed of a moving body is **doubled**, its kinetic energy becomes —
practice.solution: KE = ½mv². Doubling v multiplies v² by 2² = **4**.
practice.shortcut: KE follows the square of speed.

practice.q: A boy of mass **50 kg** runs up a staircase **12 m** high in **20 s**. Taking g = 10 m/s², his power is —
Normal human body temperature **37 °C** on the Fahrenheit scale is —
practice.solution: F = 9/5 × 37 + 32 = 66.6 + 32 = **98.6 °F**. Just adding 32 (69) is the common slip.

practice.q: At what Celsius temperature is the Fahrenheit reading **exactly double** the Celsius reading?
practice.solution: Put F = 2C in F = 9C/5 + 32: 2C − 1.8C = 32 → 0.2C = 32 → **C = 160 °C** (and F = 320 °F). −40 is where the two readings are **equal**, not double.

practice.q: A temperature of **50 °C** on the Kelvin scale is (take 0 °C = 273 K) —
practice.solution: K = C + 273 = 50 + 273 = **323 K**. (Subtracting gives 223, a common slip.)

practice.q: Food cooks faster in a **pressure cooker** because —
options: The higher pressure lowers the boiling point of water
The higher pressure raises the boiling point of water
Less water evaporates, so no heat is lost
practice.solution: Trapped steam increases pressure, so water boils at about 120 °C instead of 100 °C; the hotter water cooks food faster.

practice.q: Water kept in an **earthen pot (matka)** stays cool because of —
practice.solution: Water seeps through the pot's tiny pores and **evaporates** from the outside surface, taking latent heat from the water inside.

practice.q: Fish survive in lakes that freeze in winter because water has its **maximum density** at —
practice.solution: Water is densest at **4 °C** (anomalous expansion). Colder water and ice float on top, the ice layer insulates, and water at the bottom stays near 4 °C.

practice.q: Places near the sea have a milder climate than inland places mainly because water has a —
practice.solution: Water's **high specific heat** means the sea heats up and cools down slowly, keeping nearby land from getting very hot or very cold.

practice.q: Heat from the **Sun** reaches the Earth by —
practice.solution: Space between the Sun and the Earth is almost empty; only **radiation** needs no medium.

practice.q: A **thermos (vacuum) flask** keeps tea hot because it reduces heat loss by —
practice.solution: The vacuum between the double walls stops **conduction and convection**, and the silvered walls reflect back **radiation** — all three are reduced.

practice.q: Sound travels **fastest** in —
practice.solution: Sound is fastest in solids (steel ≈ 5000 m/s or more), slower in water (≈ 1500 m/s), slower still in air (≈ 343 m/s), and does not travel in vacuum.

practice.q: The speed of sound in air **increases** when —
options: The temperature of the air falls
Air pressure rises at constant temperature
The loudness of the sound increases
The temperature of the air rises
practice.solution: Warmer air carries sound faster (about 0.6 m/s per °C). At constant temperature, pressure changes do not affect it, and loudness has no effect on speed.

practice.q: The normal range of human hearing is —
practice.solution: Humans hear **20 Hz – 20 kHz**. Below is infrasonic, above is ultrasonic.

practice.q: The **pitch** of a sound depends on its —
practice.solution: Higher **frequency** = higher pitch (a shrill sound). Amplitude decides loudness; speed depends on the medium.

practice.q: Bats find their way in the dark using —
practice.solution: Bats emit **ultrasonic** squeaks (above 20 kHz) and listen for echoes — echolocation. The same idea is used in SONAR.

practice.q: A boy hears the echo of his shout from a cliff **2 s** later. If sound travels at **340 m/s**, the cliff is —
practice.solution: Sound travels to the cliff and back: 2d = 340 × 2 → d = **340 m**. Forgetting to halve gives 680 m.

practice.q: The whistle of an **approaching** train sounds higher-pitched than that of a receding one. This is due to —
practice.solution: When the source moves towards the listener, more waves reach per second — heard frequency rises. This is the **Doppler effect**.

practice.q: Soldiers are asked to **break step** while crossing a bridge in order to avoid —
practice.solution: Marching in step could match the bridge's natural frequency, causing large **resonant** vibrations that may damage it.

practice.q: Which mirror is used as a **rear-view mirror** in vehicles?
practice.solution: A **convex mirror** always gives an erect, diminished image with a **wide field of view**, so the driver sees more traffic behind.

practice.q: A **shaving mirror** gives an erect, magnified image of the face. It must be a —
options: Concave mirror with the face between the pole and focus
Concave mirror with the face beyond the centre of curvature
practice.solution: A **concave mirror** gives an erect, enlarged, virtual image only when the object is inside the focal length — that is how a shaving mirror magnifies the chin.

practice.q: The image formed by a **plane mirror** is always —
practice.solution: A plane mirror forms a virtual, erect image of the **same size**, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, with **left and right interchanged** (lateral inversion).

practice.q: A **magnifying glass** is a —
options: Convex lens used with the object inside its focal length
Concave lens used close to the eye
practice.solution: A **convex lens** held close to the object (within F) gives an erect, magnified, virtual image — the working of a simple microscope.

practice.q: A **concave lens**, when a real object is placed before it, always forms an image that is —
practice.solution: A diverging (concave) lens spreads the rays apart, so they only seem to meet — the image is always **virtual, erect and smaller** than the object, wherever the real object is placed.

practice.q: Which instrument produces a **real, inverted, diminished** image on a screen/film?
practice.solution: In a **camera** the object lies far beyond 2F of the convex lens, so the image is real, inverted and smaller — formed on the film or sensor. A microscope magnifies; the periscope and kaleidoscope use plane mirrors only.

practice.q: **Hypermetropia** (long-sightedness) is corrected by using a —
practice.solution: In hypermetropia the image forms **behind** the retina; a **convex (converging) lens** brings the image forward onto the retina. ('Hyper-Vex'.)

practice.q: The **least distance of distinct vision** for a normal human eye is about —
practice.solution: A normal adult eye cannot focus clearly on objects closer than about **25 cm**. The far point is at infinity.

practice.q: Why can **colour blindness** not be corrected by any lens?
options: It is caused by missing/defective colour-sensing cones in the retina
The eye lens has become opaque
practice.solution: Colour blindness is a defect of the **cones** (red–green sensors) of the retina, not of the lens or cornea, so no external lens can fix it. Cataract (opaque lens) is the only defect here treated by replacing the lens.

practice.q: The power of a **convex lens of focal length 25 cm** is —
practice.solution: 25 cm = 0.25 m; P = 1/0.25 = **+4 D** (positive because the lens is convex). Writing 1/25 = 0.04 D without converting cm to m is the common slip.

practice.q: The power of a **concave lens of focal length 50 cm** is —
practice.solution: 50 cm = 0.5 m; P = 1/0.5 = 2 D, and a concave lens takes the **negative sign**: **−2 D**.

practice.q: Sunlight takes about **8 minutes 20 seconds** to reach the Earth. The Earth–Sun distance is nearly —
practice.solution: d = c × t = (3 × 10⁸) × 500 = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m (500 s = 8 min 20 s). This distance is 1 astronomical unit.

practice.q: A pencil standing in a glass of water appears **bent** at the water surface because of —
practice.solution: Light changes speed going from water to air, so the rays bend (**refraction**) and the underwater part looks raised and bent.

practice.q: The **sparkle of a diamond** is mainly because of —
practice.solution: Diamond's very high refractive index (about 2.4) gives a small critical angle, so light entering the stone bounces inside it many times by **total internal reflection** before coming out.

practice.q: The Sun appears about **2 minutes before actual sunrise** because of —
practice.solution: Sunlight bends through the denser layers of the atmosphere, so we see the Sun's image while it is still below the horizon — about 2 minutes early (and 2 minutes late at sunset).

practice.q: **Optical fibres** carry light signals over long distances using —
practice.solution: Light entering the thin glass fibre hits its wall beyond the critical angle and is repeatedly totally internally reflected, staying inside the fibre. Endoscopes work the same way.

practice.q: **Danger signal lights are red** because red light —
options: Is least absorbed by the atmosphere
Is scattered the least and is visible from far away
practice.solution: Red has the **longest wavelength** in visible light, so air molecules scatter it least — it stays strong and visible over the greatest distance.

practice.q: In the dispersion of white light by a prism, the colour **deviated (bent) the most** is —
practice.solution: Violet has the shortest wavelength and slows the most in glass, so it bends most; red bends least. The order is VIBGYOR from the base of the spectrum upward.

practice.q: A **rainbow** is formed by —
options: Dispersion and total internal reflection of sunlight in raindrops
Refraction of sunlight in dust particles
Scattering of sunlight by air molecules
practice.solution: Sunlight entering a raindrop is dispersed, reflected inside (TIR), and leaves dispersed again — splitting into VIBGYOR. The bow is always seen with the **Sun behind** the observer.

practice.q: The **sky appears blue** because —
options: The sea reflects blue light upward
Blue light travels fastest in air
The atmosphere absorbs red light completely
Air molecules scatter blue light more than red
practice.solution: Scattering by tiny air molecules is strongest for short wavelengths, and blue/violet scatter the most — so scattered blue light reaches the eye from every direction.

practice.q: Two resistors of **4 Ω and 6 Ω** are connected in series. Their total resistance is —
practice.solution: In series, resistances simply add: 4 + 6 = **10 Ω** (2.4 Ω is what a parallel combination would give).

practice.q: Resistors of **2 Ω, 3 Ω and 6 Ω** are in parallel. The equivalent resistance is —
practice.solution: 1/R = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6 = 1, so R = **1 Ω**. In parallel the total is always less than the smallest resistor.

practice.q: By **Ohm's law**, the current through a **44 Ω** resistor connected to **220 V** is —
practice.solution: I = V/R = 220/44 = **5 A**. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 9680 — the classic trap.

practice.q: In a **series** circuit, which quantity remains the **same** through every component?
practice.solution: A series circuit offers one path, so the **same current** passes through each component; the supply voltage, however, divides among them.

practice.q: A **2000 W** heater runs for 3 hours. The electrical energy consumed is —
practice.solution: Energy = 2 kW × 3 h = **6 kWh = 6 units**. 1 unit of electricity is 1 kilowatt-hour.

practice.q: A current of **2 A** flows through a **25 Ω** resistor for **1 minute**. The heat produced is —
practice.solution: H = I²Rt = 2² × 25 × 60 = 4 × 25 × 60 = **6000 J**. Forgetting to convert 1 minute into 60 s gives 100 J.

practice.q: The filament of an electric bulb is made of **tungsten** because tungsten has —
practice.solution: The filament glows white-hot; **tungsten's very high melting point** (about 3400 °C) lets it glow without melting. Nichrome (high resistivity) is used for heating coils.

practice.q: A **fuse wire** is so designed that it —
options: Has a very high melting point
Melts quickly when the current exceeds the safe limit
Increases the current in the circuit
practice.solution: A fuse is a **low-melting-point** alloy wire (tin–lead) placed **in series with the live wire**; excess current heats and melts it, breaking the circuit.

practice.q: The direction of force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field is given by —
practice.solution: **Fleming's left-hand rule** gives the force (motor effect); the right-hand rule gives the induced current in a generator. 'Left for Motor, Right for Generator.'

practice.q: An **electric generator** converts —
practice.solution: A generator (dynamo) uses **electromagnetic induction** (Faraday, 1831): turning a coil in a magnetic field induces a current. A motor does the reverse.

practice.q: A **transformer** works —
options: On both AC and DC equally
practice.solution: A transformer works by **mutual induction**, which needs a *changing* magnetic field — so it works only on alternating current. A steady DC gives no induced voltage.

practice.q: The core of an **electromagnet** is made of **soft iron** because soft iron —
options: Magnetises quickly and loses its magnetism just as quickly
practice.solution: Soft iron is a **temporary magnet** material: it becomes a strong magnet while current flows and demagnetises when it stops — ideal for cranes and electric bells. Steel holds magnetism and makes permanent magnets.

practice.q: Household electrical appliances are connected in **parallel** because —
options: The current through each appliance is the same
Each appliance gets the full supply voltage and works independently
practice.solution: In **parallel** every branch receives the full 220 V and can be switched off alone; in series all appliances would share the voltage and one fault would stop everything.

practice.q: The colour of insulation on the **earth wire** of Indian domestic wiring is —
practice.solution: Live — red/brown, neutral — black, **earth — green**. The earth wire connects metal bodies of appliances to the ground for safety.

practice.q: The standard **AC mains supply** in Indian homes is —
practice.solution: India uses alternating current at about **220 V and 50 Hz** (the current reverses 50 times a second). 110 V/60 Hz is the American standard.

practice.q: Arranged by **increasing wavelength**, the correct order is —
options: Gamma → X-rays → UV → Visible → Infrared → Microwave → Radio
Radio → Microwave → Infrared → Visible → UV → X-rays → Gamma
X-rays → Gamma → UV → Visible → Infrared → Microwave → Radio
Visible → UV → X-rays → Gamma → Radio → Microwave → Infrared
practice.solution: Gamma rays have the shortest wavelength, radio waves the longest. Frequency increases in the reverse order. Mnemonic: 'Good X-rays Use Visible Infra-Micro Radios'.

practice.q: **Microwave ovens** and **radar** use —
practice.solution: **Microwaves** (between infrared and radio waves) are strongly absorbed by water molecules — perfect for heating food — and reflect well off objects, so radar uses them.

practice.q: **Ultraviolet** radiation falling on the skin helps produce —
practice.solution: UV-B converts a skin chemical into **vitamin D** — sunlight is the natural source. UV lamps also sterilise water and surgical tools.

practice.q: A silicon crystal doped with a **trivalent** impurity such as boron becomes —
practice.solution: Trivalent atoms (boron, gallium) leave one bond short of an electron, creating **holes** — positive carriers — so the crystal is **p-type**. Pentavalent doping (phosphorus, arsenic) gives n-type.

practice.q: A **rectifier** is a device that converts —
options: Low voltage DC into high voltage DC
practice.solution: Diodes act as **rectifiers**, turning alternating current into one-way (direct) current — chargers and power supplies do this. The reverse (DC → AC) is an inverter.

practice.q: Which subatomic particle carries a **negative** charge?
practice.solution: The **electron** (found by J.J. Thomson) is negatively charged; the proton is positive; the neutron has no charge.

practice.q: **Canal rays**, whose study led to the discovery of the proton, were observed by —
practice.solution: Goldstein's **canal rays** (anode rays) are streams of positive particles — protons. Thomson found the electron, Chadwick the neutron, Rutherford the nucleus.

practice.q: **X-rays** were discovered by —
practice.solution: **Röntgen** discovered X-rays in 1895 and received the first-ever Nobel Prize in Physics (1901). Becquerel found radioactivity; the Curies found radium.

practice.q: The existence of a small, dense, positively charged **nucleus** was established by —
practice.solution: In Rutherford's gold-foil experiment (1911) most alpha particles passed through the foil but a few bounced back, showing that nearly all the positive charge and mass sit in a tiny nucleus.

practice.q: The **telephone** was invented by —
practice.solution: **Bell** patented the telephone (1876). Edison — bulb and phonograph; Marconi — radio; Morse — telegraph.

practice.q: The **television** was invented by —
practice.solution: The Scottish inventor **John Logie Baird** demonstrated television in 1926. Marconi is radio; Faraday worked on electromagnetic induction.

practice.q: The **dynamo (electric generator)** is based on electromagnetic induction, discovered by —
practice.solution: **Faraday** discovered electromagnetic induction (1831) — a changing magnetic field induces current — the principle of the dynamo and transformer.

practice.q: Which radiation from a radioactive substance has the **greatest penetrating power**?
practice.solution: Order of penetration: **gamma (electromagnetic wave) > beta (electron) > alpha (helium nucleus)**. Alpha is stopped even by paper; gamma needs thick lead.

practice.q: **Radioactivity** was discovered by —
practice.solution: **Becquerel** noticed uranium salts emitting penetrating rays in 1896. Marie and Pierre Curie then discovered polonium and radium.

practice.q: The age of ancient organic remains is estimated by —
practice.solution: **Carbon-14 dating** (developed by Willard Libby) measures how much radioactive C-14 is left in dead organic matter.

practice.q: The energy of the **Sun** is produced by —
practice.solution: In the Sun's core, hydrogen nuclei **fuse** into helium, converting a little mass into huge energy (E = mc²).

practice.q: The **atom bomb** dropped on Hiroshima worked on —
practice.solution: The atom bomb is an uncontrolled **fission** chain reaction (U-235). The hydrogen bomb is the fusion (thermonuclear) one; a reactor is *controlled* fission.

practice.q: In a nuclear reactor, the chain reaction is controlled by inserting rods of —
practice.solution: **Control rods** of cadmium or boron absorb excess neutrons and keep the chain reaction steady. Graphite/heavy water are moderators (they slow neutrons, not absorb).

practice.q: Who is called the **father of India's nuclear programme**?
practice.solution: **Homi J. Bhabha** founded India's atomic energy effort (TIFR, BARC). Sarabhai is the father of the space programme; Kalam is the 'Missile Man'.

practice.q: India's first research reactor, **Apsara**, became critical in —
practice.solution: **Apsara** (Trombay, 1956) was India's — and Asia's — first research reactor. Tarapur (1969) was the first nuclear *power* station; 1974 was Pokhran-I.

practice.q: The first Indian satellite, launched in **1975**, was named —
practice.solution: **Aryabhata** (1975) was India's first satellite, named after the ancient mathematician. Rohini was the first carried by India's own SLV-3 (1980).

practice.q: **National Space Day** (23 August) marks —
options: Chandrayaan-3's landing near the Moon's south pole
practice.solution: On **23 August 2023** Chandrayaan-3's Vikram lander touched down near the lunar south pole — India became the first country to do so; the date is now National Space Day.

practice.q: The **first Indian to travel into space** was —
practice.solution: Sqn Ldr **Rakesh Sharma** flew to the Salyut-7 space station in 1984 on a Soviet spacecraft. Kalpana Chawla was the first woman of Indian origin in space; Shubhanshu Shukla (2025) was the first Indian on the ISS.

practice.q: The famous equation **E = mc²** was given by —
practice.solution: Einstein's mass–energy equivalence says a small mass m converts into energy E = mc², with c the speed of light — the basis of nuclear energy.

practice.q: The **'God particle'**, confirmed at CERN's Large Hadron Collider in 2012, is the —
practice.solution: The **Higgs boson**, predicted by Peter Higgs, explains how particles acquire mass. It was hunted down at the LHC in 2012.

practice.q: Laser light is used in surgery and fibre-optic communication because it is —
practice.solution: LASER = Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation: one wavelength, waves in step (coherent), and a tight beam — ideal for precision work and carrying signals along optical fibres.
